n: This Herod is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea from AD 41 to 44. He began to persecute Church leaders to win favor with the people.

f.g: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great and nephew of Herod Antipas.
Harm, mistreat.

n: James, son of Zebedee and one of the original Twelve, became the first apostle to die as a martyr. Jesus had foretold that James would share his “cup” of suffering.
Seeing that the execution was popular, Herod arrested Peter too. It was Passover season, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims — an echo of Jesus’ own arrest.
Herod placed Peter under heavy guard — sixteen soldiers in shifts — planning a public trial after the feast. “Easter” here translates the Greek word for Passover.

f.g: Four squads of four soldiers each, rotating through the night watches.
Greek pascha — Passover. Most modern translations read “Passover.”

n: Peter was locked away, but the Church prayed earnestly and constantly for him. Luke sets the contrast clearly: Herod’s power on one side, the saints’ prayers on the other.

f.g: Earnestly, intensely — the Greek suggests stretched-out, fervent prayer.

n: On the night before his trial, Peter was asleep — chained to two soldiers, with more guards at the door. His calm sleep shows remarkable trust in the Lord.
An angel appeared, light filled the cell, and he nudged Peter awake. The chains simply fell off — no human help was involved.
The angel gave simple, practical instructions: get dressed, put on your sandals, wrap your cloak around you, and follow. Heavenly help often comes with ordinary steps for us to take.

f.g: Tie up your tunic with your belt, ready to move.

n: Peter followed, but it all felt so unreal that he thought he was seeing a vision. “Wist not” means he did not realize it was actually happening.

f.g: Wist = knew; he did not know.

n: They passed two guard posts and reached the iron gate to the city, which opened by itself. After one street, the angel vanished.

f.g: Guard post or watch station.
By itself — without anyone opening it.

n: Standing in the street, Peter came to his senses. Now he knew for certain the Lord had rescued him from Herod and from what the crowds were hoping to see.

f.w: Now I know of a surety

n: Peter went to the home of Mary, mother of John Mark, where believers were praying for him. Her house seems to have been a gathering place for the Jerusalem church.

f.g: Traditionally the author of the Gospel of Mark; cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10).

n: A servant girl named Rhoda came to answer his knock at the outer gate. Luke preserves her name, a small personal touch in the story.

f.g: Young woman; here likely a household servant.
A Greek name meaning “rose.”

n: Rhoda recognized Peter’s voice and was so excited that she ran to tell everyone — leaving him standing outside. It’s a delightfully human moment.
Those praying for Peter’s release couldn’t believe it when it came! They called Rhoda crazy, then guessed it must be his “angel” — a guardian spirit, as some Jews then believed.

f.g: You’re out of your mind.
Some Jews of the time believed each person had a guardian angel who could resemble them.

n: Peter kept knocking until they finally opened the door. They were amazed to see him standing there.
Peter quieted them, told the story, and asked them to tell James and the others. This James is the Lord’s brother, now a leader in Jerusalem. Peter then went into hiding.
At dawn the soldiers were in a panic. Losing a prisoner was a serious matter for Roman-style guards.

f.g: A big commotion — Luke’s understated way of saying something major.

n: Herod searched without success and had the guards executed, as the law of the time often required for guards who lost a prisoner. Then he left for Caesarea.

f.g: The Roman administrative capital on the coast.

n: Herod was angry with the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. They depended on his territory for food, so they won over his chamberlain Blastus and asked for peace.

f.g: Phoenician port cities north of Galilee, in modern Lebanon.
Personal attendant to the king, an influential court official.

n: On an appointed day, Herod appeared in his royal robes and gave a public speech. The Jewish historian Josephus describes a robe of silver that shone in the sun.

f.g: Josephus (Antiquities 19.8.2) also records this event and Herod’s sudden death.

n: The crowd flattered him, shouting that he spoke like a god. Herod accepted the praise instead of rejecting it.
Because he took glory that belonged to God, an angel struck him, and he died a painful death. The persecutor who killed James met a swift end.

f.w: he gave not God the glory

f.g: Died; breathed his last.

n: A short but powerful summary: tyrants rise and fall, but the word of God keeps spreading. Herod is gone, and the Church grows.

f.w: the word of God grew and multiplied

n: Barnabas and Saul finished delivering the famine relief and returned to Antioch, bringing John Mark with them. This sets the stage for their first missionary journey.
